title: Programmable nonlinear function synthesis on a photonic processor with quantum signal processing
authors: Elaheh Karooby, Masoud Hakimi Heris, Yuan Liu, Qing Gu
abstract: Programmable photonic integrated circuits are emerging as increasingly large and versatile interferometric processors operating at room temperature. However, their native operations are linear, while many computational tasks require nonlinear input-output transformations that typically rely on nonlinear optical materials or resonant devices. Here, we establish a direct mapping between quantum signal processing (QSP) and the native two-mode operations of programmable interferometric photonic integrated circuits, showing that the $SU(2)$ structure required by QSP can be realized through programmable phase control and mode mixing. We experimentally demonstrate this correspondence using dual-rail single-photon encoding on a 24-mode programmable photonic integrated circuit, realizing QSP sequences up to depth $L=11$ and synthesizing STEP, ReLU and SELU functions through programmable phase control. The optical transformation remains linear, while repeated encoding of the input variable and coherent interference produce a nonlinear dependence of the output probabilities on the encoded variable. Across all accessible circuit depths, the measured responses follow the programmed QSP transformations, with hardware-induced mean squared errors between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-2}$, all remaining below the intrinsic finite-depth approximation error. These results establish an algorithm-to-hardware mapping of QSP on programmable photonic processors. They also demonstrate an algorithmic route to programmable nonlinear functions of encoded variables on linear photonic hardware.
summary: This paper demonstrates how to program nonlinear functions on a photonic processor, despite the hardware being fundamentally linear. They achieve this by mapping the problem onto Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) theory and using single-photon encoding. The results confirm that repeated interference and encoding allow the linear hardware to emulate complex nonlinear behavior with high fidelity.
main_problem: The core challenge is synthesizing complex, nonlinear input-output transformations on a photonic processor whose native operations are inherently linear.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an algorithm-to-hardware mapping, realizing and verifying programmable nonlinear functions (STEP, ReLU, SELU) using linear photonic hardware.
method: They employed Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) theory to map the desired nonlinear function onto a sequence of two-mode unitary operations achievable via programmable phase control in the photonic circuit.
model_or_system: The platform is a programmable photonic integrated circuit (PIC) utilizing dual-rail single-photon encoding and Mach-Zehnder Interferometers (MZIs). The QSP sequence is implemented by controlling programmable phase shifters.
key_observables: Output probabilities P(0) and P(1), which are used to reconstruct the function $f(x) = P(0) - P(1)$; Mean-Squared Error (MSE) quantifying accuracy.
important_parameters: Circuit depth $L$ (up to 11 demonstrated); hardware-induced mean squared errors ($10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$); input variable $x$ encoded as a phase difference.
main_assumptions: The underlying photonic transformation remains strictly linear; nonlinearity is achieved algorithmically through the QSP encoding and coherent interference.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping from classical function synthesis to the QSP rotation sequence, the experimental realization on the PIC, and the reconstruction of the output function from measured probabilities.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical mapping between QSP and two-mode photonic operations, details the experimental implementation using dual-rail encoding and programmable phase control, and validates the synthesis of specific nonlinear functions (STEP, ReLU, SELU) by measuring output probabilities.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, hardware-validated pathway to implement complex, non-linear quantum computations using linear optical components, which is a major goal in photonic quantum computing.
